newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD unveils plan for "modern state".
newsitem.headline: German SPD unveils plan for "modern state".

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrat Party (SPD), seeking to boost its chances of winning power in elections next year, on Tuesday unveiled a blueprint for a modern state to lead the country into the 21st century.
A working paper drawn up by the party's "Progress 2000" policy group calls for cutting Germany's notorious bureaucratic red-tape to make government more responsive to citizens' needs.
But the document eschews the kind of all-out privatisation pursued by other western states, instead opting for a pragmatic approach to deflating Germany's bloated welfare state.
"Only the rich can afford a weak state," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine told a party policy conference.

Lafontaine blamed Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 14-year-old conservative government for allowing a reform backlog to build up. The Bonn federal bureaucracy has swollen unchecked, spewing out a flood of new laws and regulations.
At the last count, Lafontaine said, there were 84,000 legal norms governing German life at the national level alone.
"Conservative politicians want, on ideological grounds, to force back the state ever more," said Lafontaine, who is also premier of Saarland state.
"For us, on the contrary, the question of reforming the state is not a question of ideology, but one of common sense."

The paper marks an effort to build on a threadbare SPD policy base ahead of elections in autumn 1998. Although Germans are dissatisfied with the Kohl government, polls have shown they do not see the SPD offering real alternatives.
It also plays to the SPD's strengths at the grassroots of Germany's decentralised political system. The SPD rules, alone or in coalition, in a majority of Germany's 16 federal states.
But the paper outlines no public spending targets -- while the Kohl government has pledged to reduce state spending to 46 percent of gross domestic product by the year 2000 from over 50 percent now.
Lafontaine said the planned move of the seat of federal government to Berlin in 1999 should be used "make ministries smaller and enable them to concentrate on their main tasks".
And, while pledging to crack down on the abuse of Germany's generous benefits system, Lafontaine said the welfare state as such must not be broken up.
Privatisation should only be allowed when the private sector can execute tasks more efficiently than the state.
"If the state can do better, then ideological fixation should not result in private businesses charging citizens more than necessary," Lafontaine said.
Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder -- widely seen as a potential challenger to Lafontaine as the SPD's chancellor candidate next year -- adopted a more pro-business approach.
He said the state must copy the private sector to become more efficient and rid itself of its hierarchical and authoritarian tendencies.
"If we don't turn the public sector into a customer-oriented service, we won't be able to achieve reform," he told party delegates.
That could lead to some job losses among Germany's six million state workers.
"But that is the only way out. We have already reached the limits of what we can pay for," Schroeder said.
